title: Glacier ice is blue because water itself is blue, once there’s enough of it

cover.alt: Deep blue ice inside crevasses and a cave at the foot of Fox Glacier, New Zealand.

body: Pure water is not quite colourless. Its molecules absorb a little red light, because the stretching vibration of the O–H bond has an overtone at the red end of the visible spectrum, so light that has travelled a long way through water or ice comes out faintly blue. In a glass you cannot see it: water’s blue shows only after about **3 metres** of travel. Snow and ordinary ice look white because countless air bubbles scatter all colours straight back out. Deep in a glacier the weight of snow above squeezes the bubbles out and grows large crystals, so light travels far inside before escaping, and the ice glows blue.

slides.prompt: Pure water has a colour of its own. What is it?
slides.detail: Hard to see in a glass, obvious through metres of water or dense ice. Heavy water (D2O) absorbs further into the infrared and would not look blue at all.

steps.label: Snow piles up on the glacier
Deeper layers are crushed by the weight
Ice crystals grow large and clear
Light travels far; red is absorbed

left.label: Snow
left.text: Tiny crystals and air bubbles scatter light straight back out before much red is absorbed, so every colour returns: white.

right.label: Glacier ice
right.text: Dense, bubble-free ice with big crystals lets light travel far inside; red is absorbed on the way and blue comes out.

slides.label: of water or clear ice before its blue becomes visible
slides.text: A bucket of water looks colourless; a deep indoor pool seen from above looks sky blue.

slides.alt: Inside a glacier cave: smooth blue ice walls curving overhead.
slides.caption: In an ice cave the light reaching you has passed through metres of ice.

slides.question: Exposed glacier ice turns white within hours. Why?
options: Air cracks it into small crystals
Salt from the air coats it
slides.explanation: Warmer air opens fissures that break up the big crystals and fill with air, which scatters light back out. Fresh blue shows again only where the ice breaks or an iceberg rolls over.
